deterministicSteps.title: Step 1: Output — showing things on screen
deterministicSteps.intro:
Everything useful a program does eventually needs to be shown to a person — a result, a message, a warning. That's called output. In Python, print() is the main way to produce output: it takes whatever you give it and displays it on the screen. You'll use it constantly, from your very first program onward, to check results and talk to the user.

A common beginner surprise: nothing appears unless you actually call print — just writing a value on its own doesn't display it.

open.question: In your own words: what does print() do, and why would a program need it? A short answer is fine.
open.expectedIdea: print() displays/outputs information (text or values) on the screen so a person can see it; programs need output to communicate results or messages.
acceptableAnswers: It shows text on the screen
It displays output/results so the user can see them
It prints messages to the screen so people know what happened
open.hint: print() shows information on the screen. Programs need it so they can tell the user something — a result, a message, or a check of what happened.

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: If that makes sense, we can continue — or say "another example" if you'd like one more.
deterministicSteps.summary: print() produces output — it shows information on the screen.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 2: Text and quotes
deterministicSteps.intro:
When the thing you want to show is text, Python needs to know where that text begins and ends — so you wrap it in quotes. Text inside quotes is called a string. This matters because without quotes Python thinks you are naming something and gives an error.

The quotes are just boundary markers: they tell Python "treat these characters as text," and they are not shown on screen themselves. A frequent mix-up is expecting the quotes to appear too — they do not.
deterministicSteps.example:
print("Cat")
# shows: Cat   (the quotes are not shown)

mcq.question: When you print a string, what happens to the quotation marks around it?
options: They are not shown — only the text inside appears
They are printed along with the text
mcq.correctAnswer: They are not shown — only the text inside appears
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Right — quotes just mark where text starts and ends. print("Cat") shows Cat, without quotes.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: The quotes are only markers — they are not shown. print("Cat") displays Cat, not "Cat".

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: Make sense? If so we'll keep going.
deterministicSteps.summary: Text goes in quotes; the quotes mark the text but are not printed.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 3: Reading a print line
deterministicSteps.intro:
Now let's put it together and read a print line the way Python does. The trick is simple: look inside the parentheses, and whatever text sits inside the quotes is exactly what appears — nothing more, nothing less.

This skill lets you predict a program's output before you even run it, which is how you check your own code. A common confusion is thinking the word print or the parentheses show up on screen — they don't; only the quoted text does.
deterministicSteps.example:
print("I like Python")
# shows: I like Python

mcq.question: To predict what a print line shows, what should you focus on?
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Exactly — only the text inside the quotes appears. So print("I like Python") shows I like Python.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on the text inside the quotes — that is what appears. print("I like Python") shows I like Python.

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: If that makes sense, you've reached the end of the lesson — ready to wrap up?
deterministicSteps.summary: To read a print line, focus on the text inside the quotes — that is the output.

units.deterministicOverview:
Welcome! In this lesson we'll learn how print() lets a Python program show information on the screen.

We'll go through three ideas: (1) what "output" is and why programs need it, (2) how text works with quotes, and (3) how to read a print(...) line and predict exactly what appears.

By the end you'll be able to look at a simple print line and say what it shows. Let's start with the first idea.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Text vs numbers

deterministicSteps.title: Step 1: Printing numbers directly
deterministicSteps.intro:
Numbers are values Python already understands, so you can hand them straight to print() with no quotes. This is handy any time your program computes something — a count, a total, an age — and needs to show it.

You still need the parentheses, just like with text. A common beginner habit is adding quotes out of reflex; that works visually but quietly turns a number into text, which we will look at next.

mcq.question: How do you give a whole number to print()?
options: Only after turning it into a word
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Right — numbers need no quotes. print(42) shows 42.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: Numbers go in directly, without quotes: print(42) shows 42.

deterministicSteps.summary: Numbers can be printed directly, without quotes.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 2: Numbers vs. text
deterministicSteps.intro:
Here's a subtle but important idea: print(3) and print("3") both put a 3 on screen, yet they are different things. 3 is a real number Python can do math with; "3" is just the character three, treated as text.

It matters the moment you calculate — you can add numbers but not text. A common confusion is assuming they are the same because they look alike on screen.
deterministicSteps.example:
print(3)     # the number three
print("3")   # the text "3" — looks the same, but it is text

mcq.question: print(3) and print("3") look the same on screen. What is the real difference?
options: 3 is a number Python can compute with; "3" is text
There is no difference at all
mcq.correctAnswer: 3 is a number Python can compute with; "3" is text
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Exactly — same look, different type. 3 is a number; "3" is text you cannot do math with.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: They look identical but differ in type: 3 is a number (you can do math with it), "3" is text.

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: Clear? On to the last idea.
deterministicSteps.summary: print(3) is a number; print("3") is text — same look, different type.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 3: Printing a calculation
deterministicSteps.intro:
Because numbers are real values, you can put a calculation inside print() and Python works it out first, then shows the result. This is your first taste of the computer doing something for you rather than just echoing text.

A common surprise: this only happens without quotes — print("2 + 3") would show the characters 2 + 3 as plain text instead.
deterministicSteps.example:
print(2 + 3)
# shows: 5   (Python does the math first)

open.question: What do you think print(10 + 5) shows on the screen, and why?
open.expectedIdea: It shows 15 because Python evaluates the arithmetic 10 + 5 first (they are numbers), then prints the result.
open.hint: Python does the math before printing, so print(10 + 5) shows 15 — the result of adding, not the text "10 + 5".

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: If that makes sense, you've reached the end of the lesson — ready to wrap up?
deterministicSteps.summary: Python evaluates arithmetic inside print(), so print(2 + 3) shows 5.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: A variable is a name for a value

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Use the name to get the value
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: Wherever you use the name, Python gives you its value. So print(name) shows Maya (the stored value).

knowledgeBaseChunks.content: name (no quotes) means the stored value; "name" (in quotes) is just the word name. print(name) shows Maya; print("name") shows name.

Forgetting quotes when storing text, e.g. name = Maya.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 1: A variable names a value
deterministicSteps.intro:
A variable is a name you attach to a value so you can use it later by that name. You create one with =, the name on the left and the value on the right, like score = 0. This matters because programs work with lots of values, and names make code readable and reusable instead of scattering raw values everywhere.

A common beginner confusion is reading = as "equals" like in math; here it means "store this value under this name."
deterministicSteps.example:
city = "Rome"
# the name city now holds the value Rome

mcq.question: In Python, what does the = do in  score = 0 ?
options: Stores the value 0 under the name score
mcq.correctAnswer: Stores the value 0 under the name score
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Right — = stores the value on the right under the name on the left. Now score holds 0.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: A single = stores a value: score = 0 puts 0 under the name score (it does not compare or print).

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: With me so far? Let's continue.
deterministicSteps.summary: A variable is a name for a value; = stores the value under that name.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 2: Reusing a value with its name
deterministicSteps.intro:
The real power of a variable is reuse: once a value has a name, you can use that name as many times as you like, and if the value ever changes you only update it in one place. This keeps programs short and avoids mistakes from retyping the same thing.

For example, if name = "Sam", you can greet, thank, and sign off using name without typing "Sam" three times. A common beginner habit is repeating the literal value everywhere instead of naming it once.
deterministicSteps.example:
name = "Sam"
print(name)   # Sam
print(name)   # Sam again — no retyping

open.question: Why is it useful to store a value in a variable instead of typing the same value over and over?
open.expectedIdea: Reusing a named value avoids repetition, keeps code readable, and means you only change it in one place if it needs updating.
acceptableAnswers: You can reuse it and change it in one place
It keeps code shorter and easier to update
open.hint: A variable lets you reuse the same value by name and update it in just one place — less typing and fewer mistakes.

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: If that makes sense, we can continue — or say "another example" if you'd like one more.
deterministicSteps.summary: Variables let you reuse a value by name and update it in one place.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 3: The name vs. the value
deterministicSteps.intro:
It's important to separate a variable's name from the value it holds. Without quotes, a word is treated as a variable and Python gives you its stored value; with quotes, the same word is just literal text.

Getting this right prevents a classic bug where the wrong thing prints. The common confusion is thinking the variable's name is what gets printed — it is the stored value that does.
deterministicSteps.example:
fruit = "apple"
print(fruit)     # shows: apple  (the value)
print("fruit")   # shows: fruit  (just the word)

mcq.question: After  fruit = "apple" , what does printing the variable (no quotes) give you?
options: The variable's name as a word
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Right — printing the variable gives its stored value, so print(fruit) shows apple.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: Printing the variable (no quotes) gives its stored value: print(fruit) shows apple, while print("fruit") shows the word fruit.

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: If that makes sense, you've reached the end of the lesson — ready to wrap up?
deterministicSteps.summary: A variable's name isn't printed — its stored value is.

units.deterministicOverview:
This lesson introduces variables — names you give to values so you can reuse them.

We'll cover three ideas: (1) how a variable stores a value under a name, (2) why reusing a value through its name beats repeating it, and (3) the difference between a variable's name and the value it holds.

By the end you'll be able to create a variable and use it. Let's begin.

units.title: Changing a Variable Value
units.goal: Change (update) the value in a variable by assigning it again.

teacherBrain.persona: A friendly Python instructor who teaches absolute beginners with tiny concrete steps and everyday examples.
objectives: Reassign a variable to give it a new value.
Know that the latest value wins after reassignment.
Track a changing value like a score, progress, or lives.
guidelines: Step 1: Show the example score = 1 then score = 2 exactly, and say what it does in one short sentence.
Step 2: Read it aloud in plain words (e.g. "set score to 1, then change it to 2").
Step 3: Ask the learner to try one tiny variation themselves.
Step 4: If the learner is close enough, ACCEPT it, gently clean up the wording, and continue — do not nitpick.

Step 5: If the learner says "I don't know" or is stuck, STOP asking open-ended questions: give a short DIRECT explanation with one concrete example (score = 1 then score = 2), then ask one very easy check question.
Step 6: Correct any listed common mistake right away, and do not advance until the learner answers the mastery check.
constraints: Assume earlier units in this course are done.
Teach ONLY this step; do not jump ahead to later topics.
Redirect off-topic or future-topic questions and say they come later.
Do not suggest advancing while a listed common mistake is unresolved.

Follow the flow in order: 1) show score = 1 then score = 2, 2) explain briefly, 3) let the learner try, 4) accept close answers and tidy the wording, 5) if the learner is stuck give a direct explanation plus the example score = 1 then score = 2, 6) check mastery. Advance only once the learner can reassign a variable and know the latest value wins and avoids the listed mistakes. Redirect any off-topic or later-topic question and say it comes later. knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Assigning again replaces the value
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: score = 1 stores 1. score = 2 then stores 2 in the same variable. Now score is 2 — the old 1 is gone.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: The latest value wins
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: After score = 1 then score = 2, print(score) shows 2, because a variable keeps only its most recent value.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: One value at a time
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: A variable does not keep a list of old values. It holds exactly one value: the last one you assigned.

knowledgeBaseChunks.title: Worked example
knowledgeBaseChunks.content: level = 1 then print(level) shows 1. Then level = 3 then print(level) shows 3. The second assignment replaced the first.

questions.prompt: After score = 1 then score = 2, what does print(score) show?
Start with level = 1, then change it to 3, then print it (three lines).
Mastery check: after score = 1 then score = 2, is the old value 1 still stored?
questions.answer: No — it was replaced by 2. A variable keeps only its latest value.

hints.text: Only the most recent value remains.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking both values are kept (that score = 2 adds to the old 1).
commonMistakes.correction: Reassignment REPLACES the old value. After score = 2, the 1 is gone; score holds only 2.
A single = stores a value into the variable; it does not check if two things are equal.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting print(score) to show 1 after score = 2.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 1: Giving a variable a new value
deterministicSteps.intro:
A variable isn't locked to its first value — you can give it a new one at any time, just by assigning again with =. The newer assignment simply overwrites the old value. This is essential because most real data changes: a score, a page number, a user's status.

A common confusion is expecting a second assignment to create a separate variable; it doesn't — it reuses the same name.

mcq.question: What happens when you assign a new value to a variable that already has one?
options: The new value replaces the old one
Python refuses and shows an error
mcq.correctAnswer: The new value replaces the old one
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Right — assigning again overwrites the old value. After score = 10, score holds 10.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: Assigning again reuses the same name and replaces the value: after score = 10, score holds 10.

deterministicSteps.summary: Reassigning a variable replaces its old value with a new one.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 2: The latest value wins
deterministicSteps.intro:
When a variable has been changed several times, only the most recent value survives — the earlier ones are gone, not kept in some history. So whenever you read a variable, you get its latest value, which is exactly why the order of your lines matters.

A common beginner mistake is expecting an older value to still be available; once overwritten, it is gone unless you saved it elsewhere.
deterministicSteps.example:
x = 1
x = 9
print(x)
# shows: 9   (the 1 is gone)

mcq.question: After a variable has been reassigned a few times, which value do you get when you read it?
options: The first one it ever had
mcq.feedbackCorrect: Right — only the latest value remains. After x = 1 then x = 9, x is 9.
mcq.feedbackIncorrect: You always get the latest value: after x = 1 then x = 9, reading x gives 9.

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: Clear? One more idea to go.
deterministicSteps.summary: A variable keeps only its latest value; the older ones are gone.

deterministicSteps.title: Step 3: Tracking things that change
deterministicSteps.intro:
Putting it together: because variables can change, programs use them to track state — information that evolves as the program runs. A game tracks a score and lives; a quiz tracks the current question; a download tracks progress.

Each time something happens, the program reassigns the variable to the new value. The big idea: variables give a program a memory that updates over time.
deterministicSteps.example:
lives = 3
lives = 2   # player lost one life
# lives now holds 2

open.question: Can you name something a program might track by changing a variable over time?
open.expectedIdea: Any evolving piece of state — e.g. a game score, remaining lives, download/progress percentage, current level, or number of items in a cart.
open.hint: Think of anything that changes while a program runs — a score going up, lives going down, a progress bar filling. Each is a variable that gets reassigned.

deterministicSteps.checkpointPrompt: If that makes sense, you've reached the end of the lesson — ready to wrap up?
deterministicSteps.summary: Variables let programs track changing state like score, lives, or progress.

By the end you'll understand how variables change over time. First idea coming up.
